claim: Distinct populations of Purkinje cells (PCs) with unique molecular and connectivity features are at the core of the modular organization of the cerebellum.
source: Distinct populations of Purkinje cells (PCs) with unique molecular and connectivity features are at the core of the modular organization of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific knowledge about cerebellar organization.

claim: Firing activity of PCs differs between ZebrinII-positive and ZebrinII-negative cerebellar modules.
source: Previously, we showed that firing activity of PCs differs between ZebrinII-positive and ZebrinII-negative cerebellar modules (Zhou et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Several features of PCs, including activity levels, dendritic arborization, axonal shape and climbing fiber input, develop differentially between nodular and anterior PC populations.
source: We found that several features of PCs, including activity levels, dendritic arborization, axonal shape and climbing fiber input, develop differentially between nodular and anterior PC populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All PCs show a particularly rapid development in the second postnatal week.
source: Although all PCs show a particularly rapid development in the second postnatal week, anterior PCs typically have a prolonged physiological and dendritic maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing developmental changes across different age groups.

claim: Anterior PCs typically have a prolonged physiological and dendritic maturation compared to other PC populations.
source: Although all PCs show a particularly rapid development in the second postnatal week, anterior PCs typically have a prolonged physiological and dendritic maturation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing developmental timelines between anterior and nodular PCs.

claim: Younger mice exhibit attenuated anterior-dependent eyeblink conditioning.
source: In line herewith, younger mice exhibit attenuated anterior-dependent eyeblink conditioning, but faster nodular-dependent compensatory eye movement adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Younger mice exhibit faster nodular-dependent compensatory eye movement adaptation.
source: In line herewith, younger mice exhibit attenuated anterior-dependent eyeblink conditioning, but faster nodular-dependent compensatory eye movement adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Specific cerebellar regions have unique developmental timelines which match with their related, specific forms of cerebellum-dependent behaviors.
source: Our results indicate that specific cerebellar regions have unique developmental timelines which match with their related, specific forms of cerebellum-dependent behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration of physiological, morphological, and behavioral data.

claim: The parasagittal organization of the cerebellum is fundamental to confer specificity to the coordination and adaptation of behavior.
source: The parasagittal organization of the cerebellum is fundamental to confer specificity to the coordination and adaptation of behavior.
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge about cerebellar organization.

claim: Cerebellar modules are anatomical and functional units known to control specific tasks such as limb and finger movement, compensatory eye movements, and associative motor learning.
source: This organization is based on cerebellar modules, that is, anatomical and functional units (Apps and Hawkes, 2009; Voogd, 1964; White and Sillitoe, 2013), known to control specific tasks such as limb and finger movement (Horn et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2000), compensatory eye movements (De Zeeuw and Yeo, 2005; Graham and Wylie, 2012; Voogd et al., 2012; Sugihara et al., 2004), and associative motor learning (Attwell et al., 2001; Hesslow and Ivarsson, 1994; Jirenhed et al., 2007; Mostofi et al., 2010; Raymond et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Purkinje cells from different modules express different levels of molecular markers such as ZebrinII.
source: Purkinje cells (PCs) from different modules not only express different levels of molecular markers (Apps and Hawkes, 2009; Cerminara et al., 2015), such as ZebrinII (Brochu et al., 1990), but also have different physiological properties (Xiao et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), project to discrete targets in cerebellar and vestibular nuclei (Garwicz and Ekerot, 1994; Sugihara et al., 2009), receive climbing fiber (CF) input from unique subnuclei of the inferior olive (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007a; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004), are linked to specific muscle groups (Ruigrok, 2011; Ruigrok et al., 2008) and are differentially predisposed to degeneration in neurodegenerative mouse models (Sarna and Hawkes, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Purkinje cells from different modules have different physiological properties.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PCs contribute to the proliferation of granule cells through the release of Sonic Hedgehog.
source: For example, PCs contribute to the proliferation of granule cells through the release of Sonic Hedgehog (Lewis et al., 2004), as well as the parasagittal organization of afferents (Arsénio Nunes et al., 1988) and interneurons (Sillitoe et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PCs contribute to the parasagittal organization of afferents.
source: For example, PCs contribute to the proliferation of granule cells through the release of Sonic Hedgehog (Lewis et al., 2004), as well as the parasagittal organization of afferents (Arsénio Nunes et al., 1988) and interneurons (Sillitoe et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PCs contribute to the parasagittal organization of interneurons.
source: For example, PCs contribute to the proliferation of granule cells through the release of Sonic Hedgehog (Lewis et al., 2004), as well as the parasagittal organization of afferents (Arsénio Nunes et al., 1988) and interneurons (Sillitoe et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Transient disruptions in PC development can have lasting effects and influence the development of other brain areas.
source: Recent evidence suggests that transient disruptions in PC development can have lasting effects and influence the development of other brain areas (Badura et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The timing of PC birth is related to its ultimate placement in the cerebellar cortex, with earlier born PCs settling generally more laterally than later born PCs.
source: The timing of the PC birth is related to its ultimate placement in the cerebellar cortex, with earlier born PCs settling generally more laterally than later born PCs (Hashimoto and Mikoshiba, 2003; Namba et al., 2011; Sillitoe et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A precise reorganization from embryonic clusters of PCs into the parasagittal stripes of the mature cerebellum is indicative of a very straightforward process from embryonic origins into mature modules.
source: Additionally, a precise reorganization from embryonic clusters of PCs into the parasagittal stripes of the mature cerebellum is indicative of a very straightforward process from embryonic origins into mature modules (Fujita et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: By postnatal day 12, it is possible to observe ZebrinII expression-related differences in firing rate of both simple spikes and complex spikes.
source: In vivo recordings revealed that by postnatal day (P) 12 it is possible to observe ZebrinII expression-related differences in firing rate of both simple (SSs) and complex spikes (CSs), and in vitro recordings in ZebrinII-positive (Z+) lobule X and ZebrinII-negative (Z–) lobule III confirmed that these differences are intrinsically driven as reported in the adult mouse and rat (Xiao et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differences in firing rate between ZebrinII-positive and ZebrinII-negative PCs at P12 are intrinsically driven.
source: In vivo recordings revealed that by postnatal day (P) 12 it is possible to observe ZebrinII expression-related differences in firing rate of both simple (SSs) and complex spikes (CSs), and in vitro recordings in ZebrinII-positive (Z+) lobule X and ZebrinII-negative (Z–) lobule III confirmed that these differences are intrinsically driven as reported in the adult mouse and rat (Xiao et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both PC populations differ in their timeline of dendritic maturation from P18.
source: Furthermore, we show that both PC populations also differ in their timeline of dendritic (from P18) and axonal (from P14) maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both PC populations differ in their timeline of axonal maturation from P14.
source: Furthermore, we show that both PC populations also differ in their timeline of dendritic (from P18) and axonal (from P14) maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CF translocation appears to occur earlier in the nodular regions by P7.
source: CF translocation appears to occur earlier in the nodular regions (by P7) further suggesting differences of developmental timelines between distinct cerebellar regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Young animals (P21-P25), compared to adults, display more effective adaptation of compensatory eye movements.
source: Finally, we show that young animals (P21-P25), compared to adults, display more effective adaptation of compensatory eye movements, which is controlled by Z+ modules in the vestibulocerebellum (Zhou et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Compensatory eye movement adaptation is controlled by Z+ modules in the vestibulocerebellum.
source: Finally, we show that young animals (P21-P25), compared to adults, display more effective adaptation of compensatory eye movements, which is controlled by Z+ modules in the vestibulocerebellum (Zhou et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Young animals show a reduction in their learning rate during eyeblink conditioning.
source: In contrast, young animals show a reduction in their learning rate during eyeblink conditioning, which is linked to anterior Z– modules (Hesslow and Ivarsson, 1994; Mostofi et al., 2010), further supporting the emerging concept of differences in circuitry maturation in distinct cerebellar regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Eyeblink conditioning is linked to anterior Z– modules.
source: In contrast, young animals show a reduction in their learning rate during eyeblink conditioning, which is linked to anterior Z– modules (Hesslow and Ivarsson, 1994; Mostofi et al., 2010), further supporting the emerging concept of differences in circuitry maturation in distinct cerebellar regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PC subpopulations' developmental timelines shape unique cerebellar circuitries that underlie different maturational profiles of specific cerebellar functions.
source: Overall, this study shows for the first time that PC subpopulations' developmental timelines shape unique cerebellar circuitries that underlie different maturational profiles of specific cerebellar functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration of physiological, morphological, and behavioral data.

claim: SS firing rate is significantly higher in Z− PCs when compared with Z+ PCs in all age groups, starting from early postnatal ages (P12-P17).
source: We observed that SS firing rate is significantly higher in Z− PCs when compared with the Z+ PCs in all age groups, starting from early postnatal ages (P12-P17, Z−: 57.3 ± 5.3 Hz, Z+: 42.3 ± 5.7 Hz, p=0.013, see Supplementary file 1 for additional age groups).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: Z– PCs significantly increase their firing rate progressively from P12 until reaching their mature rate.
source: Moreover, Z– PCs significantly increase their firing rate progressively from P12 until reaching their mature rate (P12-P17, Z– vs. >P60 Z–: p<0.0001) while Z+ PCs firing rate remained low and plateaued at P18, which is not significantly different from the rate at the mature stage (P18-P29 Z+ vs. Z+:>P60 Z+: p=0.185) (Figure 1B1,C1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A3, Supplementary file 1 for additional age groups).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: Z+ PCs firing rate remained low and plateaued at P18, which is not significantly different from the rate at the mature stage.
source: Moreover, Z– PCs significantly increase their firing rate progressively from P12 until reaching their mature rate (P12-P17, Z– vs. >P60 Z–: p<0.0001) while Z+ PCs firing rate remained low and plateaued at P18, which is not significantly different from the rate at the mature stage (P18-P29 Z+ vs. Z+:>P60 Z+: p=0.185) (Figure 1B1,C1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A3, Supplementary file 1 for additional age groups).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: There is no difference in SS regularity (CV2) in the young P12-P17 group between Z– and Z+ PCs.
source: Although there is no difference in SS regularity, measured as coefficient of variation 2 (CV2), in the young P12-P17 group (CV2, Z–: 0.51 ± 0.03, Z+: 0.51 ± 0.04, p=0.94), there is a significant difference between Z– and Z+ PC regularity in the older groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: From P18 onwards, Z– PCs are more irregular than Z+ PCs.
source: From P18 onwards, Z– PCs are more irregular than Z+ PCs (>P60, Z–: 0.47 ± 0.01, Z+: 0.40 ± 0.01, p<0.001) (Figure 1C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: The CS activity of Z+ PCs is significantly reduced compared with Z– PC CSs in adulthood, a difference that becomes evident from as early as P18-P27.
source: As expected, the CS activity of Z+ PCs is significantly reduced compared with Z– PC CSs in adulthood, a difference that becomes evident from as early as P18-P27 (Z–: 1.50 ± 0.15 Hz; Z+: 1.14 ± 0.08 Hz, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: CS activity of Z+ PCs at P12-P17 is significantly higher when compared with Z– PC CSs.
source: In marked contrast, CS activity of Z+ PCs at P12-P17 is significantly higher when compared with Z– PC CSs (Z–: 0.79 ± 0.09 Hz; Z+: 1.06 ± 0.11 Hz, p=0.011) (Figure 1D1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: There is no significant difference in CF pause in young cells P12-P17 between Z– and Z+ PCs.
source: While there is no significant difference in CF pause in young cells P12-P17 (Z–: 81.1 ± 12.7 msec; Z+: 79.6 ± 13.8 msec, p=0.94), there is a significant increase in CF pause of Z+ PCs when compared with Z– PCs at P18, after synapse elimination, that is maintained into adulthood (>P60, Z–: 20.0 ± 0.8 msec; Z+: 34.5 ± 2.4 msec, p<0.0001) (Figure 1D2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: There is a significant increase in CF pause of Z+ PCs when compared with Z– PCs at P18, after synapse elimination, that is maintained into adulthood.
source: While there is no significant difference in CF pause in young cells P12-P17 (Z–: 81.1 ± 12.7 msec; Z+: 79.6 ± 13.8 msec, p=0.94), there is a significant increase in CF pause of Z+ PCs when compared with Z– PCs at P18, after synapse elimination, that is maintained into adulthood (>P60, Z–: 20.0 ± 0.8 msec; Z+: 34.5 ± 2.4 msec, p<0.0001) (Figure 1D2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: PCs are intrinsically active in the absence of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs.
source: PCs are intrinsically active in the absence of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs (De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Raman and Bean, 1999; Womack and Khodakhah, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The difference in PC SS firing rate recorded in vivo was primarily the result of intrinsic activity of PCs in the adult mouse.
source: In our previous work, we found that the difference in PC SS firing rate recorded in vivo was primarily the result of intrinsic activity of PCs in the adult mouse (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: PC firing rate significantly increases from P3-P5 to P10-P11 in both lobule III and lobule X.
source: PC firing rate significantly increases from P3-P5 to P10-P11 (LIII p=0.0002; LX p=0.0007), but over these first days of development there were no differences in the firing rate between PCs of different cerebellar regions (Figure 2A2,B1-Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claim: Over the first days of development (P3-P5 to P10-P11) there were no differences in the firing rate between PCs of different cerebellar regions.
source: PC firing rate significantly increases from P3-P5 to P10-P11 (LIII p=0.0002; LX p=0.0007), but over these first days of development there were no differences in the firing rate between PCs of different cerebellar regions (Figure 2A2,B1-Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claim: Starting from P12 to P17, the intrinsic activity of PCs located in lobule X is significantly different from those located in lobule III.
source: Starting from P12 to P17, similar to the in vivo data, we observed that the intrinsic activity of PCs located in lobule X is significantly different from those located in lobule III (LIII: 51.7 ± 3.4 Hz; LX: 34.8 ± 2.0 Hz, p=0.008, Figure 2B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claim: After P12-P17, the differences in intrinsic firing rate in PCs from both cerebellar regions are maintained into adulthood.
source: After this key point during development, the differences in intrinsic firing rate in PCs from both cerebellar regions are maintained into adulthood (>P60, LIII: 61.2 ± 2.5 Hz; LX: 46.3 ± 1.9 Hz, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claim: There is a significant increase in irregularity in lobule III PCs from P18 when compared with lobule X PCs.
source: In line with the in vivo results (Figure 1B2), there is a significant increase in irregularity in lobule III PCs from P18 when compared with lobule X PCs (CV2, LIII: 0.11 ± 0.01; LX: 0.05 ± 0.00, p<0.0001) and this is maintained into adulthood (>P60, CV2, LIII: 0.11 ± 0.01; LX: 0.04 ± 0.00, p<0.0001) (Figure 2B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claim: Differences in SS firing rate at least in lobules III and X are indeed the result of differences of intrinsic activity of distinct PC subpopulations starting at P12-P17 and maintained into mature ages.
source: All together, these data indicate that differences in SS firing rate at least in lobules III and X are indeed the result of differences of intrinsic activity of distinct PC subpopulations starting at P12-P17 and maintained into mature ages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro recording data.

claim: From P6-P11 to P12-17 there is a rapid increase in dendritic complexity and area across all PCs.
source: Concomitantly with the physiology data, we observed that from P6-P11 to P12-17 there is a rapid increase in dendritic complexity and area (Figure 3A) across all PCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claim: There is no significant difference in dendritic complexity, maximum length, and area between PCs in anterior (lobules I/II/III) and nodular (lobules IX/X) regions at P12-P17.
source: However, unlike in the physiological data there is no significant difference in dendritic complexity (P12-P17, LI-III: 336.1 ± 31.7; LIX-X: 291.2 ± 17.1, p=0.38, Figure 3B1), maximum length (P12-P17, LI-III: 138.3 ± 5.1 µm; LIX-X: 142.5 ± 3.9 µm, p=0.74, Figure 3B2), and area (P12-P17, LI-III: 5419 ± 399 µm2; LI-X: 6109 ± 462 µm2, p=0.46, Figure 3B3) between PCs in anterior (lobules I/II/III) and nodular (lobules IX/X) regions at P12-P17.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claim: Dendritic arborization in lobules IX-X marginally changed after P12-P17.
source: While dendritic arborization in lobules IX-X marginally changed after this time point, dendritic complexity significantly increased in lobules I-III from the third postnatal week (from P18) into adulthood: dendritic complexity (P60, LI-III: 663.1 ± 23.8; LIX-X: 445.7 ± 22.2, p<0.0001, Figure 3B1), maximum length (P60, LI-III: 206.6 ± 5.9 µm; LIX-X: 169.9 ± 4.0 µm, p<0.0001, Figure 3B2), and area (P60, LI-III: 10890 ± 412 µm2; LIX-X: 8520 ± 377 µm2, p<0.0001, Figure 3B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claim: Dendritic complexity significantly increased in lobules I-III from the third postnatal week (from P18) into adulthood.
source: While dendritic arborization in lobules IX-X marginally changed after this time point, dendritic complexity significantly increased in lobules I-III from the third postnatal week (from P18) into adulthood: dendritic complexity (P60, LI-III: 663.1 ± 23.8; LIX-X: 445.7 ± 22.2, p<0.0001, Figure 3B1), maximum length (P60, LI-III: 206.6 ± 5.9 µm; LIX-X: 169.9 ± 4.0 µm, p<0.0001, Figure 3B2), and area (P60, LI-III: 10890 ± 412 µm2; LIX-X: 8520 ± 377 µm2, p<0.0001, Figure 3B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claim: A difference in size and complexity in dendritic arborization of PC subpopulations can be first observed at P18.
source: A difference in size and complexity in dendritic arborization of PC subpopulations can therefore be first observed at P18 (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claim: At P7 there was a significant increase in VGluT2 puncta in lobules IX-X when compared with lobules I-III.
source: Remarkably, we found that at P7 there was a significant increase in VGluT2 puncta in lobules IX-X (P7, LI-III: 0.62 ± 0.31%; LIX-X: 3.87 ± 0.19%, p<0.0001, Figure 4B2) when compared with lobules I-III.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: At P7 the percentage of CF extension into the molecular layer was significantly increased in lobules IX-X compared to lobules I-III.
source: As a result, at P7 the percentage of CF extension into the molecular layer (ML) was significantly increased in lobules IX-X (P7, LI-III: 11.1 ± 1.1%; LIX-X: 80.5 ± 1.0%, p<0.0001, Figure 4B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: CF translocation starts earlier in nodular lobules.
source: These results suggest that CF translocation starts earlier in nodular lobules (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemical data on VGluT2 puncta and CF extension.

claim: From P7 to P14, there was a dramatic increase in ML thickness in both regions of the cerebellum.
source: From P7 to P14, there was a dramatic increase in ML thickness in both regions of the cerebellum (Figure 4B1) but the significant difference in VGluT2 puncta and CF terminals disappeared (VGluT2 puncta, P7: p<0.0001, P14: p=0.78; CF terminals, P7: p<0.0001, P14: p=0.24, Figure 4B2 and B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: From P21 into adulthood, there was a significant increase in ML thickness in lobules I-III when compared with the nodular lobules.
source: From P21 into adulthood, there was a significant increase in ML thickness in lobules I-III when compared with the nodular lobules (P60, LI-III: 137.5 ± 1.3 µm; Lob IX-X: 116.9 ± 4.9 µm, p<0.001, Figure 4B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: CF translocation into the PC dendrite starts earlier in nodular lobules when compared with anterior lobules I, II, and III.
source: These results indicate that CF translocation into the PC dendrite starts earlier in nodular lobules when compared with anterior lobules I, II, and III pointing to another difference in the maturation of the cerebellar circuitries in different cerebellar regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemical data on CF development.

claim: PC axons are present in the cerebellar nuclei as early as embryonic day (E) 15.5 in mice.
source: PC axons are present in the cerebellar nuclei as early as embryonic day (E) 15.5 in mice (Sillitoe et al., 2009) and E18 in rats (Eisenman et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Targeting to the correct cerebellar subnuclei is already in place at very early points in cerebellar development.
source: Targeting to the correct cerebellar subnuclei is also already in place at very early points in cerebellar development (Sillitoe et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PC axons exhibit a multi-step developmental process in culture.
source: In culture, PC axons exhibit a multi-step developmental process (de Luca et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There are significant differences across age of PC axon arbor maximum length and complexity, as both parameters increase from P7 to P14 and then decrease at P21.
source: This analysis revealed significant differences across age of PC axon arbor maximum length and complexity, as both parameters increase from P7 to P14 and then decrease at P21 (number of intersections, P7: 84.2 ± 18.2; P10: 254.4 ± 40.5; P14: 277.4 ± 17.5; P21: 296.4 ± 37.9, p=0.013; length, P7: 124.2 ± 17.8 µm; P10: 212.7 ± 24.4 µm; P14: 216.4 ± 14.3 µm2; P21: 225.2 ± 16.1 µm2, p=0.060, Figure 5C,E1, E2).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claim: Area taken up by the axon arbors continued to increase with age.
source: Area taken up by the axon arbors, however, continued to increase with age (area, P7: 1.52 ± 0.20 µm2·103 P10: 1.47 ± 0.25 µm2·103; P14: 2.26 ± 0.19 µm2·103; P21: 3.07 ± 0.29 µm2·103, p<0.0001; Figure 5E3).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claim: Sholl analysis revealed significant differences between Z– and Z+ axon arbors at P10, P14 and P21, with Z– axon arbors exhibiting a denser branching complexity than Z+.
source: Sholl analysis revealed significant differences between Z– and Z+ axon arbors at P10, P14 and P21, with Z– axon arbors exhibiting a denser branching complexity than Z+ (P10: p=0.0457; P14: p=0.0017; P21: p=0.0388).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claim: Significant differences were found between Z– and Z+ groups for length and area but not number of intersections.
source: Significant differences were found between Z– and Z+ groups for length and area but not number of intersections (intersections, p=0.252; length, p=0.0197; area, p=0.0257; Figure 5F1-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claim: PC axons reach near mature shapes already early in development, with a peak in size around P14 and subtle differences between Z– and Z+ axons.
source: Taken together, our novel approach to analyze axon terminal development in cerebellar nuclei indicates that PC axons reach near mature shapes already early in development, with a peak in size around P14 and subtle differences between Z– and Z+ axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological data on axon arbor development.

claim: The VOR ensures the stabilization of images on the retina via compensatory eye movement every time the vestibular system is activated.
source: The VOR ensures the stabilization of images on the retina via compensatory eye movement every time the vestibular system is activated (head movement).
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge about the VOR.

claim: VOR adaptation is the adjustment of compensatory eye movements based on a mismatch between vestibular and visual input.
source: VOR adaptation is the adjustment of compensatory eye movements based on a mismatch between vestibular and visual input, moving in the same or opposite direction (i.e. in or out of phase) (Ito, 1982; Nagao, 1989; Schonewille et al., 2010; Wulff et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations.

claim: Compensatory eye movements are controlled by the flocculus, together with the nodulus forming the vestibulocerebellum, which is predominantly Z+.
source: Moreover, compensatory eye movements are controlled by the flocculus, together with the nodulus forming the vestibulocerebellum, which is predominantly Z+ (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Hawkes and Herrup, 1995; Sillitoe and Hawkes, 2002; Figure 6A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the EBC paradigm, a neutral sensory stimulus alone leads to a well-timed eyeblink after repeated pairing with a noxious stimulus which induces a reflexive eyelid closure.
source: In the EBC paradigm, a neutral sensory stimulus alone leads to a well-timed eyeblink after repeated pairing with a noxious stimulus which induces a reflexive eyelid closure (usually a mild airpuff) (Boele et al., 2010; McCormick and Thompson, 1984; Thompson and Steinmetz, 2009).
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge and is supported by citations.

claim: The cerebellar eyeblink regions putatively reside in the anterior cerebellum, in particular at the border of lobule IV-V to VI, and from the hemisphere lobule IV-V to simplex, a region that is largely ZebrinII-negative.
source: The cerebellar eyeblink regions putatively reside in the anterior cerebellum, in particular at the border of lobule IV-V to VI, and from the hemisphere lobule IV-V to simplex, a region that is largely ZebrinII-negative (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Hawkes and Herrup, 1995; Sillitoe and Hawkes, 2002; Heiney et al., 2014; Figure 6B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neither the OKR gain or phase differ significantly between juvenile and adult age groups.
source: Neither the OKR gain or phase differ significantly between age groups (OKR gain, young: 0.60 ± 0.09; adult: 0.59 ± 0.10, p=0.84; and OKR phase, young: −15.5 ± 6.7; adult: −15.4 ± 5.0, p=0.96, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A1,B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claim: The VOR gain is significantly increased in adult mice when compared with juveniles.
source: In contrast, the VOR gain is significantly increased (VOR gain, young: 0.42 ± 0.09; adult: 0.61 ± 0.09, p<0.0001, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A2) and the VOR phase decreased (VOR phase, young: 29.4 ± 5.8; adult: 21.4 ± 4.5, p=0.0024, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B2) in adult mice when compared with juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claim: The VOR phase is decreased in adult mice when compared with juveniles.
source: In contrast, the VOR gain is significantly increased (VOR gain, young: 0.42 ± 0.09; adult: 0.61 ± 0.09, p<0.0001, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A2) and the VOR phase decreased (VOR phase, young: 29.4 ± 5.8; adult: 21.4 ± 4.5, p=0.0024, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B2) in adult mice when compared with juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claim: There are no differences in the VVOR phase between juvenile and adult mice.
source: Moreover, while there are no differences in the VVOR phase (VVOR phase, young: 1.33 ± 0.46; adult: 1.35 ± 0.13, p=0.97, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B3), there is a significant increase in the VVOR gain of juvenile animals compared with adults (VVOR gain, young: 0.89 ± 0.01; adult: 0.96 ± 0.01, p=0.009, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claim: There is a significant increase in the VVOR gain of juvenile animals compared with adults.
source: Moreover, while there are no differences in the VVOR phase (VVOR phase, young: 1.33 ± 0.46; adult: 1.35 ± 0.13, p=0.97, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B3), there is a significant increase in the VVOR gain of juvenile animals compared with adults (VVOR gain, young: 0.89 ± 0.01; adult: 0.96 ± 0.01, p=0.009, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from compensatory eye movement recordings.

claim: The training resulted in juvenile animals reversing their VOR phase faster with significantly lower gain values on the first 3 days and higher phase values on all days.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that the training resulted in juvenile animals reversing their VOR phase, probed in the dark with only vestibular stimulation, faster with significantly lower gain values on the first 3 days and higher phase values on all days (VOR gain, days 1–3, all p<0.01 phase reversal, all p<0.0001, Figure 6A2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from VOR phase reversal training.

claim: Consolidation is significantly larger in juvenile mice than in adult mice, for gain decrease and for phase increase.
source: Consolidation is significantly larger in juvenile mice than in adult mice, for gain decrease (p=0.0005) and for phase increase (p=0.0006 and p=0.0069, respectively, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from VOR phase reversal training.

claim: Juvenile animals exhibit a significantly lower CR percentage after the first day of learning when compared with the adult animals.
source: Juvenile animals exhibit a significantly lower CR percentage after the first day of learning (juvenile: 20.4 ± 4.4%; adult: 30.9 ± 6.0%, p=0.027, Figure 6B2) when compared with the adult animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from eyeblink conditioning.

claim: The amplitude of the eyelid closure in response to the conditioned stimulus is reduced in juvenile animals.
source: Moreover, the amplitude of the eyelid closure in response to the conditioned stimulus (fraction eyelid closure) is reduced in juvenile animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A2,C1,C2,C3,C4).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from eyeblink conditioning.

claim: The difference in CR percentage was not due to reduced eyelid closure abilities in juvenile mice because UR timing and onset is similar between the two groups.
source: The difference in CR percentage was not due to reduced eyelid closure abilities in juvenile mice because UR timing and onset is similar between the two groups (UR onset, young: 5.61 ± 0.15; adult: 6.41 ± 0.10, p=0.41; UR peak time, young: 67.2 ± 1.0; adult: 69.0 ± 1.0, p=0.55, Figure 6—figure supplement 4A1,B1,B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from eyeblink conditioning.

claim: Juvenile animals had an attenuated rate of EBC acquisition while the VOR adaptation was heightened in juvenile animals when compared with adult animals.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that juvenile animals had an attenuated rate of EBC acquisition while the VOR adaptation was heightened in juvenile animals when compared with adult animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Different developmental timelines in distinct cerebellar regions underlie the emergency of cerebellar specific behaviors.
source: This suggests different developmental timelines in distinct cerebellar regions underlie the emergency of cerebellar specific behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration of physiological, morphological, and behavioral data.

claim: Different subpopulations of PCs acquire unique morphological and physiological features during distinct developmental timelines, such that PCs of the posterior cerebellum, particularly lobule X, reach their adult stage prior to PCs of the anterior, in e.g. lobule III, cerebellum.
source: In this study, we uncover that different subpopulations of PCs acquire unique morphological and physiological features during distinct developmental timelines, such that PCs of the posterior cerebellum, particularly lobule X, reach their adult stage prior to PCs of the anterior, in e.g. lobule III, cerebellum (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: Cerebellar compartmentalization has been shown to correlate with PCs birth dates: early-born (E10-E11.5) will become adult Z+ PCs and late-born (E11.5-E13) will become adult Z– PCs.
source: Cerebellar compartmentalization has been shown to correlate with PCs birth dates: early-born (E10-E11.5) will become adult Z+ PCs and late-born (E11.5-E13) will become adult Z– PCs (Hashimoto and Mikoshiba, 2003; Namba et al., 2011; Larouche and Hawkes, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is a strong relationship between embryonic compartments and adult zonal patterning associated with the modular organization of the olivo-cortico-nuclear circuit.
source: Thus, there is a strong relationship between embryonic compartments and adult zonal patterning associated with the modular organization of the olivo-cortico-nuclear circuit (Brochu et al., 1990; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007a; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Voogd et al., 2003; Pijpers and Ruigrok, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The maturation of the zonal phenotype is only complete around P12-P15, based on the molecular markers ZebrinII or PLCβ4.
source: The maturation of the zonal phenotype is only complete around P12-P15, based on the molecular markers ZebrinII (Brochu et al., 1990; Lannoo et al., 1991) or PLCβ4 (76).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lobule X/Z+ PCs reached adult stable properties earlier than anterior lobule III/Z– PCs, particularly when it comes to simple and complex spike activity, as well as dendritic morphology.
source: In our studies, developmental electrophysiological and morphological analyses revealed that lobule X/Z+ PCs reached adult stable properties earlier than anterior lobule III/Z– PCs (Figure 7), particularly when it comes to simple and complex spike activity, as well as dendritic morphology.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: The configuration of mature PCs follows directly from their development, which is a consequence of their birthdate.
source: This suggests that the configuration of mature PCs follows directly from their development, which is a consequence of their birthdate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the developmental data and previous research on PC birthdates.

claim: Signs of ZebrinII-related differentiation in the electrophysiological properties could already be detected in the end at the second postnatal week from P12.
source: Signs of ZebrinII-related differentiation in the electrophysiological properties, similar to those observed in firing rate of SS in the adult mouse in vivo (Zhou et al., 2014), could already be detected in the end at the second postnatal week from P12 (Figure 1C1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: Z+ PCs demonstrate early maturation of their physiological properties by reaching a SS activity level in vivo at P18 that is not significantly different from that in adulthood.
source: Z+ PCs demonstrate early maturation of their physiological properties by reaching a SS activity level in vivo at P18 that is not significantly different from that in adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: In PCs from anterior regions of the cerebellum the activity continues to gradually increase until adulthood.
source: Contrarily, in PCs from anterior regions of the cerebellum the activity continues to gradually increase until adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: CS activity also showed reduced activity of Z+ PCs compared with Z– PC CSs from P18-P27.
source: Similarly, CS activity, which results exclusively from the activity of neurons in the inferior olive, also showed reduced activity of Z+ PCs compared with Z– PC CSs from P18-P27 (Figure 1D1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: Physiological differences in two populations of PCs are first detected at the end of the second postnatal week and result from intrinsic differences combined with an input component.
source: Overall, physiological differences in two populations of PCs are first detected at the end of the second postnatal week and result from intrinsic differences combined with an input component (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the physiological data.

claim: Changes in physiological properties during development match the time course of dendritic growth in rats.
source: Previous reports have shown that, in rats, changes in physiological properties during development match the time course of dendritic growth, without differentiating subtypes (McKay and Turner, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Starting from P18, PCs of the anterior lobule III continue to grow and develop a larger dendritic area and more elaborated dendritic tree when compared with the nodular lobule X PCs.
source: Starting from P18, PCs of the anterior lobule III continue to grow and develop a larger dendritic area and more elaborated dendritic tree when compared with the nodular lobule X PCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claim: PCs in the nodular lobule X region appear to reach their adult stage at P18, although a smaller growth is still present from the adolescent to adult stage.
source: Similar to our physiology data, PCs in the nodular lobule X region appear to reach their adult stage at P18, although a smaller growth is still present from the adolescent to adult stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claim: In some populations of PCs their maturation is not only linked with their location in the cerebellum, but also coupled to their physiological development.
source: This suggests that in some populations of PCs their maturation is not only linked with their location in the cerebellum (Altman, 1972), but also coupled to their physiological development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between physiological and morphological development.

claim: Mossy fiber and CF afferents terminate into parasagittal domains that align with the ZebrinII domains.
source: In particular, mossy fiber (Sotelo and Wassef, 1991; Voogd and Ruigrok, 1997; Ji and Hawkes, 1995; Armstrong et al., 2009) and CF (Voogd and Ruigrok, 1997; Chédotal et al., 1997; Sotelo and Chedotal, 2005) afferents terminate into parasagittal domains that align with the ZebrinII domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CF development has been carefully described.
source: CF development has been carefully described (Watanabe and Kano, 2011; Hashimoto et al., 2009; Kano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CF translocation occurs earlier in the nodular lobule X cerebellar region.
source: Concomitantly with early maturation of the nodular lobule X described previously also CF translocation occurs earlier in this cerebellar region (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: The CS rate has never been found to be higher during development than in adulthood.
source: Although PCs during development are innervated by multiple CFs (Hashimoto et al., 2009; Hashimoto and Kano, 2005), the CS rate has never been found to be higher during development than in adulthood (Arancillo et al., 2015; Sokoloff et al., 2015; Kawamura et al., 2013), and we verify that here for both Z+ and Z– populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and data from the current study.

claim: CF pause duration is normalized after the period of synapse elimination at P18.
source: Our data also reveal that CF pause duration is normalized after the period of synapse elimination at P18 (Figure 1D2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo recordings.

claim: Initial dendritic outgrowth is known to be independent of input signals.
source: Initial dendritic outgrowth is known to be independent of input signals (Sotelo and Arsenio-Nunes, 1976; Alvarado-Mallart and Sotelo, 1982; Dusart et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CFs are necessary to complete PC dendritic growth and synapse maturation.
source: However, CFs are necessary to complete PC dendritic growth and synapse maturation (Sotelo and Arsenio-Nunes, 1976; Sotelo, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Positional cues from PCs are necessary for the correct CF-PC connection.
source: Moreover, positional cues from PCs are necessary for the correct CF-PC connection (Chédotal et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: During the second postnatal week features substantial changes in PC axon arbors as well.
source: During the second postnatal week features substantial changes in PC axon arbors as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data on axon arbor development.

claim: Complexity and length of PC axon arbors both significantly increase between P7 and P10 and P14.
source: Complexity and length both significantly increase between P7 and P10 and P14.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claim: Between P14 and P21, morphological pruning appears to take place in PC axon arbors.
source: However, between P14 and P21, morphological pruning appears to take place (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claim: PC axons in culture feature a multi-step development, first extending neurites and then switching to an arborizing phase.
source: PC axons in culture also feature a multi-step development, first extending neurites and then switching to an arborizing phase (de Luca et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PC axons in the adult feature differences between subnuclei of the cerebellar nuclei.
source: PC axons in the adult feature differences between subnuclei of the cerebellar nuclei (Sugihara et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Axons within the dentate nucleus exhibit very compact arbors, while axons within the medial nucleus are not dense.
source: While axons within the dentate nucleus exhibit very compact arbors, axons within the medial nucleus are not dense.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The differences between Z– and Z+ axon arbor subpopulations appear to be set early on and growth takes place within that difference already existing.
source: The differences between the subpopulations appear to be set early on and growth takes place within that difference already existing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological data on axon arbor development.

claim: The cerebellar cortex is divided rostrocaudally into four transverse zones (anterior, central, posterior, and nodular) and mediolaterally into parasagittal stripes.
source: In mammals, the cerebellar cortex is divided rostrocaudally into four transverse zones (anterior, central, posterior, and nodular) and mediolaterally into parasagittal stripes (Hawkes and Eisenman, 1997; Ozol et al., 1999; Armstrong and Hawkes, 2000; Armstrong et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both transverse and parasagittal compartments can be distinguished by gene expression.
source: Both transverse and parasagittal compartments can be distinguished by gene expression.
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Analyses of the meander tail and lurcher mutant mice have revealed a genetic compartmental boundary between nodular and anterior lobules.
source: Analyses of the meander tail (Ross et al., 1990) and lurcher (Tano et al., 1992) mutant mice have revealed a genetic compartmental boundary between nodular and anterior lobules.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A recent single-cell RNA-sequencing study has shown gene expression correlated or anti-correlated with the ZebrinII pattern.
source: Consistent with this notion, a recent single-cell RNA-sequencing study has shown gene expression correlated or anti-correlated with the ZebrinII pattern (Rodriques et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A second spatial gene expression pattern was identified related to the vestibulocerebellar region (lobules IX and X), in which genes are exclusively expressed within or outside this region.
source: A second spatial gene expression pattern was identified related to the vestibulocerebellar region (lobules IX and X), in which genes are exclusively expressed within or outside this region (Rodriques et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Studies suggest that specification of PC subpopulations (both transversal and parasagittal subtypes of PCs) is regulated by cell autonomous mechanisms, more so than activity or afferent dependent, starting from the birth of the PCs.
source: Studies suggest that specification of PC subpopulations (both transversal and parasagittal subtypes of PCs) is regulated by cell autonomous mechanisms, more so than activity or afferent dependent, starting from the birth of the PCs (Hashimoto and Mikoshiba, 2003; Namba et al., 2011; Larouche and Hawkes, 2006; Chung et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PC birthdating experiments revealed that the eight clusters of PCs identified embryonically were unchanged until adulthood.
source: Hashimoto and Mikoshiba, 2003 PC birthdating experiments revealed that, in contrast with the expression of the markers available at the time, the eight clusters of PCs the authors identified embryonically were unchanged until adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neurogranin was shown to be expressed from E14.5 in a pattern that was maintained until P20.
source: Although ZebrinII is a 'late-onset' parasagittal marker, others, such as neurogranin (Larouche et al., 2006), were shown to be expressed from E14.5 in a pattern that was maintained until P20.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Slc1a6 mRNA can already by detected from embryonic ages and immunohistochemical analysis supports a patterned, selective expression in the caudal cerebellum from embryonic day 18.
source: While Slc1a6 expression is similar to that of ZebrinII in adult mice, its mRNA can already by detected from embryonic ages and immunohistochemical analysis supports a patterned, selective expression in the caudal cerebellum from embryonic day 18 (Yamada et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PLCβ4 expression is restricted to the Z– cells and its expression also begins just before birth.
source: Additionally, PLCβ4 expression is restricted to the Z– cells and its expression also begins just before birth.
evidence: This statement draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The PLCβ4-positive clusters in the neonate are complementary with the Z– neurons.
source: The PLCβ4-positive clusters in the neonate are complementary with the Z– neurons (Marzban et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The birth date-related PCs correlated with the zonal pattern of ZebrinII.
source: With the use of mouse genetics (Sillitoe et al., 2009) or adenovirus tracing (Namba et al., 2011) it was possible to verify that the birth date-related PCs correlated with the zonal pattern of ZebrinII.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The nodulus (vermal lobule X) and the flocculus are distinct divisions of the cerebellum at an early age.
source: Finally, it is known that the nodulus (vermal lobule X) and the flocculus are distinct divisions of the cerebellum at an early age (Fujita et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Differences in SS firing rate result from intrinsic properties of PCs early in development.
source: Our electrophysiological data add to this notion that differences in physiological properties result from intrinsic properties of PCs (Figure 2) early in development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claim: Intrinsic activity could be observed as early as P3 and differences between PC subpopulations become apparent starting from P12.
source: Intrinsic activity could be observed as early as P3 and differences between PC subpopulations become apparent starting from P12.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro recordings.

claim: The influence of extrinsic inputs is relatively small in the second week, but starts to drive activity at P18.
source: Moreover, we observed that the influence of extrinsic inputs, the net effect of excitatory and inhibitory inputs, is relatively small in the second week, but starts to drive activity at P18.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing in vivo and in vitro recordings.

claim: The net driving effect of extrinsic inputs remains relatively stable in nodular lobule X/Z+ PCs.
source: While this influence remains relatively stable in nodular lobule X/Z+ PCs, the net driving effect of extrinsic inputs increases over time for anterior lobule III/Z– PCs until the cells reach their full maturation in the adult (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing in vivo and in vitro recordings.

claim: The net driving effect of extrinsic inputs increases over time for anterior lobule III/Z– PCs until the cells reach their full maturation in the adult.
source: While this influence remains relatively stable in nodular lobule X/Z+ PCs, the net driving effect of extrinsic inputs increases over time for anterior lobule III/Z– PCs until the cells reach their full maturation in the adult (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing in vivo and in vitro recordings.

claim: Z– PCs have a higher expression of TRPC3 and its ablation decreases their firing rate to make them more similar to the firing rate of Z+ PCs with behavioral consequences.
source: For instance, Z– PCs have a higher expression of TRPC3 (44) and its ablation decreases their firing rate to make them more similar to the firing rate of Z+ PCs with behavioral consequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The TRPC3 channel molecular cascade includes proteins expressed in parasagittal bands such as mGluR1b, IP3R1, PLCβ3/4, and PKCδ.
source: Additionally, the TRPC3 channel molecular cascade includes proteins expressed in parasagittal bands such as mGluR1b (Mateos et al., 2000), IP3R1 (Furutama et al., 2010), PLCβ3/4 (Sarna et al., 2006), and PKCδ (Barmack et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Specific ATPases and potassium channels were identified in Z– PCs that can contribute to explain intrinsic differences.
source: Recently, specific ATPases and potassium channels were identified in Z– PCs that can also contribute to explain intrinsic differences (Rodriques et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: From the second postnatal week PCs develop their characteristic dendritic tree coupled with functional transitions.
source: As described previously (McKay and Turner, 2005; Bradley and Berry, 1979), from the second postnatal week PCs develop their characteristic dendritic tree coupled with functional transitions (Dusart and Flamant, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Coupled with their electrophysiological properties, nodular lobule X PCs reach maturity of their dendritic tree faster than anterior lobule III PCs.
source: Our data show for the first time that coupled with their electrophysiological properties, nodular lobule X PCs reach maturity of their dendritic tree faster than anterior lobule III PCs (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis.

claim: Corticonuclear topography is related with the topography of the olivocerebellar pathway.
source: Corticonuclear topography is related with the topography of the olivocerebellar pathway (Sugihara et al., 2009; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007a), in that Z+ PCs typically project to the lateral/caudoventral cerebellar nuclei while Z– neurons typically project to the medial/rostrodorsal parts of the cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Z+ PCs typically project to the lateral/caudoventral cerebellar nuclei while Z– neurons typically project to the medial/rostrodorsal parts of the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Corticonuclear topography is related with the topography of the olivocerebellar pathway (Sugihara et al., 2009; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007a), in that Z+ PCs typically project to the lateral/caudoventral cerebellar nuclei while Z– neurons typically project to the medial/rostrodorsal parts of the cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In adult rats, PC axon arbors have been shown to vary morphologically based on their location within the cerebellar nuclei with more Z+ subnuclei containing denser, more complex PC axonal arbors.
source: In adult rats, PC axon arbors have been shown to vary morphologically based on their location within the cerebellar nuclei with more Z+ subnuclei containing denser, more complex PC axonal arbors (Sugihara et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There exists a similar pattern of distinct morphology of PC axons in the different subnuclei during development.
source: Our data shows for the first time the existence of a similar pattern of distinct morphology of PC axons in the different subnuclei during development (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data from Sholl analysis of axon arbors.

claim: VOR adaptation is controlled by the flocculus of the vestibulocerebellum, which is a Z+ region.
source: VOR adaptation and EBC are regulated by different modules in the cerebellum: VOR adaptation is controlled by the flocculus of the vestibulocerebellum, which is a Z+ region (Zhou et al., 2014; Sugihara and Quy, 2007b; Lisberger, 1988; Ito, 2002; Fujita et al., 2014), and EBC is controlled by the hemispheric lobule VI, which is predominantly a Z– region (Mostofi et al., 2010; Boele et al., 2010; Thompson and Steinmetz, 2009; Heiney et al., 2014; Hesslow, 1994a; Hesslow, 1994b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: EBC is controlled by the hemispheric lobule VI, which is predominantly a Z– region.
source: VOR adaptation and EBC are regulated by different modules in the cerebellum: VOR adaptation is controlled by the flocculus of the vestibulocerebellum, which is a Z+ region (Zhou et al., 2014; Sugihara and Quy, 2007b; Lisberger, 1988; Ito, 2002; Fujita et al., 2014), and EBC is controlled by the hemispheric lobule VI, which is predominantly a Z– region (Mostofi et al., 2010; Boele et al., 2010; Thompson and Steinmetz, 2009; Heiney et al., 2014; Hesslow, 1994a; Hesslow, 1994b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different elements of the nodular Z+ circuitry mature, that is reach their adult levels at the juvenile (P21) stage, earlier than anterior Z– circuitries.
source: Our data show that different elements of the nodular Z+ circuitry mature, that is reach their adult levels at the juvenile (P21) stage, earlier than anterior Z– circuitries and hence we hypothesize that this differentiation would manifest itself in the ability to perform related learning tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integration of physiological and morphological data.
